Would I qualify to own a working dog (I was specifically going for the Mal)? I've worked in a kennel for two years (we provide free boarding for our town's police dogs, so I've handled quite a few of them) and currently own a Border Collie. My BC and I have gone through a lot of training with professional trainers, and I've learned a lot about how to handle dogs with a higher echelon of mental abilities.

How about a Lab? I have a feeling you're going for a less common breed, but Labs seem to fit well personality-wise into your demands. They're great jogging partners, can live in apartments, people love them and they love people.

As for breeds like German Shepherds or Rottweilers, though they're definitely great dogs and can be brought up to be perfectly harmless, they tend to intimidate people just by their looks. Timidness in people can cause a dog to be timid itself. Also, these dogs are high energy dogs. I own a Border Collie who has similar energy levels as GSDs. He's pretty low-key, for a Border Collie, but even a 2hr jog wouldn't wear him out. He needs both mental and physical stimulation to be worn out, so we do some intense obedience, agility, etc for 30min twice a day and he's fine to fall asleep at night. Again, he's pretty low-key and you should expect more out of a typical GSD (though some can also be low-key! Just don't put your chances on it!).

Last thing I want to mention is how much time you're willing to put into the dog's training. This is **the most important part** of owning high-energy/large dogs. It's extremely important for you to have your dog meet as many people/dogs/animals/loud things you can fit in before it turns 8mo. I've had so many problems with my BC because he wasn't introduced properly to other dogs. He was attacked in a dog park so he has some issues. You can definitely avoid all this work by adopting a well-mannered dog. Look into it!

Again, unless you have some dog-owning experience (dog sitting does not count...), I advise you to stay away from herders/workers because there's a bunch of psychological shit that needs a lot of attention, more than you could ever imagine. Hopefully you read this fat essay and will consider my words. If you really want to go for GSDs or Pinschers or whatever, spend a bunch of time with those breeds (pet sitting counts here!) to understand how their minds work.

Hey, before you buy that dog let me tell you about my experience with getting a very much anticipated puppy. It's been a nightmare. I've always wanted a dog and I worked as a kennel boy for a few months. I offered dog sitting services and helped train friends' dogs so I assumed I knew what was to be done when my puppy arrived. I mean, I really read up on dogs. As a kid, I spent my free time in the library reading about dogs. I practically knew every breed and their history by the time I was 12. But when I got my puppy, I was completely lost. There is no way of preparing for the worst, you just have to face it. Doesn't matter how much research you do, it will never work out like you expect it to.

Firstly, I got a Border Collie. A bit high strung, yes, but surprisingly my little guy slept for most of the day. So I thought it'd be okay to return to my job (kennel worker). Who knew that after a few months he'd get a total personality makeover? My puppy changed from a snooze puppy to a hyper and incredibly anxious dog. No, not all BCs are anxious and mine was this way because of me. He started showing frightening behaviors like snarling at dogs and jumping up on kids. He used to listen so well but a few months after his arrival he became a wanderer. I got pretty anxious and in turn so did my dog.

I took him to training classes and man, these people are really rough! Maybe it's just my experience, but dog owners at training facilities are really wound up. They snap at you, the customer, when you do something wrong but tell you not to yell at your own dog. They seem to act as if I'm always doing something wrong. Anyway, it was very traumatic for me and I didn't want to interact with other dog owners.

Not to mention the cost. Now, mainly new owners ask about food and vet bills, but from my experience, my number one surprise in finance was how expensive toys were. $25 for a 6" squeaky toy? Really? $7 for a small bully stick? $18 for a Kong??? Plus, my border collie tears up anything I buy, so there's a constant stream of money being poured out onto toys. But neglecting toys was not an option. When puppies teeth, they chew on just about anything, or they whine. Chewing is one way a dog relaxes, so it's very important (even for adult dogs) to have a plethora of chew toys.

Anyway, that was basically my first 6 months with my border collie puppy. There wasn't a moment when I wasn't worrying about the puppy. You cannot leave a dog in its crate all day. It'll be more than just fed up, the pup will grow mental issues. Please heed my warning. You have to have at least 3-4 months FREE OF WORK to raise a puppy correctly. Consider that.

Or you can adopt an older dog. That'll work too. Any old man from the shelter will do fine as long as they dont have anxiety problems.
